instruction: Design a single-page introduction screen for a colorful side-scrolling platform adventure inspired by classic mascot platformers. Include a bold original game title, a hero beside a layered level preview with platforms, blocks, coins, enemies, and a distant goal, plus a prominent Start Adventure button, small controls guide, world selector, and collectible counters. Put strong emphasis on a joyful original identity, clear gameplay storytelling, depth, expressive shapes, and a polished launch-screen composition.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: the core requirement — a hero beside a layered level preview with platforms, blocks, coins, enemies, and a distant goal — is effectively unmet: the preview canvas is pushed below the fold and only a sliver of cloud/sky is visible, so the bee mascot, the goal flag, and all gameplay storytelling are absent from the launch composition. Counters, controls, world selector, and the Start CTA are present, but title/panel polish cannot excuse the missing scene. Clarity: the world-selector cards are broken — label boxes overlap the thumbnails at inconsistent heights, 'Candy Cliffs' and 'Starfall Caves' text clip at card edges, and the check badges (yellow vs green) have no explained meaning; the tip line says '→ to zoom the meadow,' contradicting the controls list (→ = move/run) and undermining the guide; the 'Live preview' label sits at the bottom edge with nothing visible to preview; the right panel reads as a settings sidebar rather than part of the game. Visual System & Craft: the background is a flat blue gradient with zero parallax or environmental layers, directly contradicting the brief's 'depth' emphasis; the left column has a large dead zone between the tip line and the level label; the title treatment (chunky outlined alternating letters) is genuinely strong, but the overall two-column 'hero text + sidebar' layout is a generic menu pattern; the rainbow stripe and keycaps are nice details that don't compensate for the missing stage. Expressiveness: identity is carried almost entirely by the title and three tiny thumbnails; the meadow world, sky, clouds, and mascot are absent from the main stage, so there is no memorable moment (no hero pose, no spinning coin, no distant flag) and the screen feels like a menu rather than a place. Real trade-offs: the oversized title + paragraph + dual buttons consume the viewport and push the scene out; the narrow right panel forces the world cards to clip; keeping all required modules (counters, controls, selector, CTA) while making the scene the focal point requires re-prioritizing the layout, not adding more polish.
history.suggestion: One prioritized plan, all achievable with inline CSS/SVG (no external assets): 1) Rebuild the layout as a single 100vh stage: make the layered level preview the dominant element — a full-width canvas band occupying the lower ~55% of the viewport, drawn in inline SVG/CSS with 2-3 parallax layers (far hills, drifting clouds, near grass), platforms, ?-style blocks, spinning coins, one 'grumble' enemy, a distant goal flag on the right, and the bee hero standing on a platform at left-center; add subtle idle motion (cloud drift, coin spin, hero bob) so 'Live preview' is true. 2) Shrink the title to ~65% of its current size and anchor it top-left over the sky, keeping the chunky outlined style, badge, and a two-line description; keep Start Adventure as the single dominant CTA with How to Play secondary, and fold the tip line into the controls area. 3) Fix the world cards: fixed card height, thumbnail on top, name + difficulty on a solid chip below (no overlapping boxes), consistent badge semantics (green check = unlocked, lock = locked, ring = selected), and eliminate all text clipping. 4) Correct the tip copy to '← → run · Space hop (hold = higher)' to match the controls list. 5) Add depth to the background behind the UI: soft sun glow, two cloud layers, and a faint hill silhouette so the flat blue gradient becomes an environment. 6) Keep the top-right collectible counters and the right panel's controls + progress, but give the panel more width or move 'World Progress' under the world cards with breathing room, so the panel reads as a game HUD rather than a settings sidebar. This preserves every required module, makes the hero + level preview the focal point, fixes the clipping/copy jank, and turns the screen from a generic menu into a place.
